people.name: Esther Agbaje
body: In the summer of 2020, a first-time candidate for a House seat covering parts of downtown and North Minneapolis took on an established incumbent. Esther Agbaje defeated four-term Rep. Raymond Dehn in the August 11 primary with 48 percent of the vote, then won in November. When she took office in January 2021, Voice of America reported that she had become the first Nigerian American to serve in the Minnesota House of Representatives.

Agbaje was born in St. Paul on March 19, 1985. Both of her parents were born in Nigeria and met as students at the University of Minnesota. Her father is an Episcopal priest; her mother worked in homeless services and as a librarian. Agbaje understands Yoruba. She attended Shattuck-St. Mary's School in Faribault, then earned degrees at George Washington University, the University of Pennsylvania and Harvard Law School.

Before politics, she worked for the U.S. State Department on rule-of-law projects in the Middle East. Back in Minnesota, she practiced as a plaintiff's attorney at Ciresi Conlin and volunteered with the Hennepin County Housing Court Project, advising people facing eviction. She was on the team in a class action against the Minnesota Department of Corrections seeking hepatitis C medication for prisoners; a settlement before trial required treatment at all stages of the disease, and Minnesota Lawyer named the team an Attorney of the Year for 2019.

When the pandemic ended door-knocking in 2020, her campaign held meet-and-greets in parks and helped constituents by phone, and during the unrest after George Floyd's murder her team made wellness calls instead of campaign calls. She was reelected in 2022 and 2024 and was an assistant majority leader in the 2023–2024 session. As of October 2026 she is in her third term and is a co-vice chair of the House Ways and Means Committee. Her term runs to January 3, 2027, and House seats are on the ballot on November 3, 2026.
keyFacts: 1985 (March 19): Born in St. Paul to parents born in Nigeria.
Education: George Washington University (B.A.), University of Pennsylvania (M.P.A.), Harvard (J.D.).
Worked for the U.S. State Department on Middle East projects.
August 2020: Defeated a four-term incumbent in the DFL primary for House District 59B.
January 2021: Took office, reported by Voice of America as the first Nigerian American in the Minnesota House.
As of October 2026: Third term; co-vice chair, House Ways and Means.
people.connectToWork: Agbaje had to change how she reached people when door-knocking stopped. When your usual way of reaching people fails, how do you find out what would work for them, rather than recording that they did not respond?

people.name: Fatima T. Lawson
body: When Highwood Hills Elementary in St. Paul was struggling, its principal, Dr. Fatima Lawson, began by listening to families. By the Star Tribune's account, the school adopted a polytechnic approach at the urging of Somali, Karen and Hispanic families. In 2024 she received the National Distinguished Principal Award, presented by the National Association of Elementary School Principals and the Minnesota Elementary School Principals' Association.

Lawson was born and raised in Kano, in northern Nigeria. A 2023 profile by Margaret McNamara Education Grants says Western education there was forbidden or discouraged, particularly for girls. She earned an undergraduate degree in French and Portuguese and a graduate degree in linguistics at the University of Ife, then a Ph.D. in education policy and administration at the University of Minnesota in 1995.

Before Highwood Hills she was for 12 years the principal of a St. Paul language immersion school she helped start, which that profile calls one of the most successful in the city. She has also taught as an adjunct professor at Twin Cities institutions. Beyond school she has chaired the board of Minnesota Africans United, served as vice president of the Minnesota Institute for Nigeria's Development and on the Governor's Council for Minnesotans of African Heritage for two terms, and been an officer of the Books For Africa board (Secretary in a 2023 profile, Treasurer on Books For Africa's 2024 page), helping organize a shipment of 50,000 books mainly to girls' secondary schools in Kano.
As of October 2026 the school lists her as its administrator, and it reports that she was named a Bush Fellow and received an award from the African Mental Health Summit.
keyFacts: Born and raised in Kano, northern Nigeria; degrees from the University of Ife.
Master's degree and Ph.D. from the University of Minnesota.
12 years as principal of a St. Paul language immersion school she helped start.
2024: National Distinguished Principal Award, at Highwood Hills.
Board chair of Minnesota Africans United; Books For Africa board officer.
2026: Named a Bush Fellow, the school reports.
people.connectToWork: Families changed the direction of Highwood Hills. In a service you work on, what could the people using it change, and how would they know you had asked?

people.name: Josh Okogie
body: On a 2011 visit to Nigeria, a teenage Josh Okogie heard advice from his uncle: if you ever get the chance to play for Nigeria, take it. Ten years later he did. In the summer of 2021, while a member of the Minnesota Timberwolves, Okogie traveled to the Tokyo Olympics with Nigeria's national team, which had just beaten the United States in an exhibition game.

Okogie was born in Lagos on September 1, 1998. When he was three, his family won a U.S. visa lottery and emigrated; aunts, uncles and grandparents stayed in Nigeria. He grew up in Snellville, Georgia, and starred at Georgia Tech, averaging 16.9 points per game over two seasons. On draft night in 2018, the Timberwolves chose him 20th overall, and he spent his first four NBA seasons in Minneapolis. He later played for Phoenix, Charlotte and Houston, and as of October 2026 he is with the Utah Jazz.
keyFacts: 1998 (September 1): Born in Lagos; family moved to the U.S. when he was three.
Played college basketball at Georgia Tech.
2018: Drafted 20th overall by the Minnesota Timberwolves; played four seasons there.
2021: Played for Nigeria at the Tokyo Olympics while a Timberwolf.
As of October 2026: Utah Jazz.
people.connectToWork: Does a form or record you use ask for one country, one home or one nationality? What does it lose about someone whose family and loyalties sit in two places, and could you ask instead of choosing for them?

people.name: Daniel Oturu
body: In December 2017, a WCCO camera crew sat with the Oturu family in their Minnesota home. Daniel, a senior at St. Paul's Cretin-Derham Hall, had just become the first in his class to commit to the University of Minnesota Gophers. The family is from Nigeria. His father, Francis, moved to the United States first, and about seven years passed before the family's older daughter joined him. The reporters noted the family's heights too: his father stands 5 foot 5, his mother, Deborah, 6 foot 1.

Oturu was born in Brooklyn, New York, on September 20, 1999. He stayed home to play for the Gophers, where he was named All-Big Ten and to the Big Ten All-Defensive Team for 2019–20. In the 2020 NBA draft the Minnesota Timberwolves selected him 33rd overall, and he began his NBA career with the Los Angeles Clippers, later playing briefly for Toronto. He then played in Turkey for Merkezefendi and Anadolu Efes, and in July 2025 he signed a three-year contract with Hapoel Tel Aviv in Israel.
keyFacts: 1999 (September 20): Born in Brooklyn; parents Deborah and Francis Oturu are from Nigeria.
Played at Cretin-Derham Hall in St. Paul.
December 2017: First in his senior class to commit to the Gophers.
2020: All-Big Ten, Big Ten All-Defensive Team, drafted 33rd overall.
2025 (July): Signed a three-year deal with Hapoel Tel Aviv.
people.connectToWork: This family spent about seven years apart while one parent moved first. When a record shows gaps or a household that changes over time, how would you ask about it without treating it as a problem to explain?

people.name: Ifeadi Odenigbo
body: As a boy in Centerville, Ohio, Ifeadi Odenigbo wanted to play football, and his parents were cautious. So he made a deal with his father: earn a 3.5 GPA or better as a freshman and he could play. He made the grade.

His mother, Linda, a pediatrician, came to the U.S. in 1992 and did her residency at Harlem Hospital Center; his father, Thomas, a civil engineer, made his final move about three years later. Ifeadi was born in New Jersey, the first member of his family born in the United States, and the family settled in Centerville when he was in first grade. He played at Northwestern University and finished second in school history with 23.5 sacks.

In 2017 the Minnesota Vikings drafted him in the seventh round, 220th overall. He spent his rookie season on the practice squad, was cut in 2018 and moved through practice squads in Cleveland and Arizona before landing back in Minnesota, then broke through in 2019 with seven sacks, third on the team. In the Chicago Sun-Times he said, "Nigerian immigrants are all about academics." That is his view of his own upbringing, and it does not describe any other family.
keyFacts: Born in New Jersey to parents Linda, a pediatrician, and Thomas, a civil engineer.
Raised in Centerville, Ohio, from first grade.
Played at Northwestern; finished second in school history in sacks (23.5).
2017: Drafted by the Minnesota Vikings, seventh round, 220th overall.
2019: Seven sacks, third on the team.
people.connectToWork: A parent's job or schooling can tell you little about what a family wants for a child. When you are working with parents and a young person who may want different things, how do you hear both?

people.name: Hakeem Olajuwon
body: As a teenager in Lagos, Hakeem Olajuwon played soccer as a goalkeeper and handball, not basketball. He did not take up the game until age 15, when a fellow student asked the coach to let him play. Within a few years he was recruited to the University of Houston. He was named Most Outstanding Player of the 1983 Final Four even though Houston lost the title game to North Carolina State, 54–52.

The Houston Rockets made him the first overall pick of the 1984 NBA draft, and he played 17 seasons for them. In 1993–94 he became the first player to win the league MVP, Defensive Player of the Year and Finals MVP in the same season, leading Houston to its first championship. The Rockets won again in 1995, and he was again Finals MVP.

Olajuwon became a naturalized U.S. citizen in April 1993 and won an Olympic gold medal with the United States in 1996 in Atlanta. He was inducted into the Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame in 2008.
keyFacts: 1963 (January 21): Born in Lagos.
1984: First overall pick in the NBA draft.
1993 (April): Became a naturalized U.S. citizen.
1994: League MVP, Defensive Player of the Year and Finals MVP; NBA champion 1994 and 1995.
1996: Olympic gold medal with the United States; 2008: Hall of Fame.
people.connectToWork: Olajuwon took up basketball at 15 and rose to the top of the game. Where does your work assume a skill has to be learned early or in a certain order, and who does that leave out?

people.name: Bennet Omalu
body: In 2002, in the Allegheny County coroner's office in Pittsburgh, a young forensic pathologist examined the brain of Mike Webster, a former Pittsburgh Steelers player who had died at 50. Dr. Bennet Omalu found a buildup of tau protein. He named the condition chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, and in 2005 published his findings in the journal Neurosurgery. By Biography.com's account, the NFL's brain injury committee called his research flawed and demanded a retraction. He did not retract it.

Omalu was born in 1968 in Nnokwa, Nigeria, during the Nigerian Civil War (1967–1970), to parents who were refugees from the war. He has described himself as a lonely, malnourished child who turned to learning. He earned his medical degree at the University of Nigeria in 1990 and came to the U.S. for further training, including time at the University of Washington, a residency at Harlem Hospital Center and a neuropathology fellowship at the University of Pittsburgh, completed in 2002. He later earned a master's degree in public health and an MBA from Carnegie Mellon.

In 2007 he became chief medical examiner of San Joaquin County, California, and he has taught pathology at UC Davis. He co-founded the Sports Legacy Institute, later renamed the Concussion Legacy Foundation. The 2015 film Concussion, starring Will Smith, brought his story to a wide audience.
keyFacts: 1968: Born in Nnokwa, Nigeria, during the civil war, to refugee parents.
1990: Medical degree, University of Nigeria.
2002: Examined Mike Webster's brain in Pittsburgh and identified CTE.
2005: Published his findings in Neurosurgery.
2015: His story was dramatized in the film Concussion.
people.connectToWork: A powerful committee told a newcomer to the field that his findings were wrong. When someone trained elsewhere brings your team evidence that does not fit, what would make you take it seriously before you judge it?

people.name: Uzo Aduba
body: In 2015, for the second year in a row, Uzo Aduba walked to the Emmy stage for the same television role, this time in the drama category rather than comedy. BroadwayWorld lists her as one of only two actors to win in both categories for the same role.

The daughter of Nigerian immigrants, Aduba grew up in Medfield, Massachusetts. Her mother braided green and white beads, the colors of the Nigerian flag, into her and her sister's hair. When classmates mocked her, once with a racial slur, she kept it from her parents so she would not add to their struggles. Her first name, Uzoamaka, roughly means "the road is good" in Igbo, which she says really means the journey was worth it.

Aduba graduated from Boston University's School of Fine Arts and worked in theater, including the 2011 Broadway revival of Godspell. Her breakthrough came as Suzanne Warren in Netflix's Orange Is the New Black, which brought Emmys in 2014 and 2015. In 2020 she won a third Emmy for playing Shirley Chisholm, the first Black woman elected to Congress, in Mrs. America. She was nominated again in 2021 for In Treatment and in 2025 for The Residence. In September 2024 she released a memoir, The Road Is Good, dedicated to her mother, Nonyem Aduba, who died of pancreatic cancer in 2020.
keyFacts: Daughter of Nigerian immigrants; raised in Medfield, Massachusetts. Uzoamaka is an Igbo name.
Graduate of Boston University's School of Fine Arts.
2014 and 2015: Emmys for Orange Is the New Black, in comedy and then drama.
2020: Emmy for playing Shirley Chisholm in Mrs. America.
2024 (September): Published the memoir The Road Is Good.
people.connectToWork: Aduba's name carries a meaning she can explain, and she kept harassment from her parents to protect them. How does your team learn to say a person's name correctly, and how would you make it safe for someone to tell you what they have been keeping to themselves?

people.name: Nnedi Okorafor
body: Nnedi Okorafor was born on April 8, 1974, in Cincinnati, Ohio, to Igbo Nigerian parents. Her parents came to the United States in 1969 to study and could not go home because of the Biafran War. Her first name, Nnedimma, means "mother is good."

She was diagnosed with scoliosis at 13. At 19, spinal fusion surgery led to a rare complication that left her paralyzed from the waist down. A long hospital stay brought months of severe pain and isolation; writing became her way through it, and the athlete became a writer. With intensive physical therapy she learned to walk again with a cane. She went on to earn degrees from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, a master's in journalism from Michigan State University, and a master's and Ph.D. in English from the University of Illinois at Chicago.

Her fiction sets science fiction and fantasy in and around Nigeria. Who Fears Death won the 2011 World Fantasy Award for Best Novel. Her novella Binti won the Nebula Award for 2015 and the 2016 Hugo Award, and in 2020 she won a second Hugo, for the graphic story LaGuardia. Her honors also include the Wole Soyinka Prize for African Literature for Zahrah the Windseeker. She taught at Chicago State University and the University at Buffalo, and in 2021 became a professor of practice at Arizona State University. She coined the term "Africanfuturism" for her kind of speculative fiction, and has collaborated with Marvel.
keyFacts: 1974 (April 8): Born in Cincinnati to Igbo Nigerian parents who arrived in 1969.
Age 19: Paralyzed after scoliosis surgery; learned to walk again with a cane.
2011: World Fantasy Award for Who Fears Death.
2015–2016: Nebula and Hugo Awards for Binti.
2020: Hugo Award for LaGuardia.
2021: Professor of practice, Arizona State University.
people.connectToWork: A hospital stay turned Okorafor from an athlete into a writer. When you meet someone after a change in their body or health, how do you find out what they want next, instead of assuming what they have lost?

people.name: Teju Cole
body: Teju Cole was born in 1975 in Kalamazoo, Michigan, to Nigerian parents, and moved with his family to Lagos at four months old. He grew up there and returned to Michigan for college at Kalamazoo College. He went on to study African art history at the School of Oriental and African Studies in London and art history at Columbia University.

His first book, Every Day Is for the Thief (2007), is set in Lagos. His second, Open City (2011), is set in New York; it won the 2012 Hemingway Foundation/PEN Award. He followed with essays (Known and Strange Things), a book pairing photographs with text (Blind Spot), and Human Archipelago, a meditation on refugees made with photographer Fazal Sheikh. His own site says his books have been published in twenty languages.

From 2015 to 2019 he was the photography critic for The New York Times Magazine. In January 2019 he joined Harvard as its first Gore Vidal Professor of the Practice of Creative Writing, the title his site lists as of October 2026. He is an elected member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters.
keyFacts: 1975: Born in Kalamazoo, Michigan, to Nigerian parents; raised in Lagos.
2007: Published Every Day Is for the Thief.
2011: Published Open City, which won the Hemingway Foundation/PEN Award in 2012.
2015–2019: Photography critic, The New York Times Magazine.
2019: Became Harvard's first Gore Vidal Professor of the Practice of Creative Writing.
people.connectToWork: Cole was born in the U.S. and raised in Lagos. Where does your work treat birthplace as a stand-in for language, schooling or sense of home, and what would you ask instead?

people.name: Babatunde Olatunji
body: In 1959 Columbia Records released an album of West African drumming called Drums of Passion. Its leader was Babatunde Olatunji, a Nigerian who had come to the United States as a college student. The album sold millions of copies around the world.

Olatunji was born on April 7, 1927, in Ajido, a fishing village in the Badagry area about 40 miles from Lagos, into a Yoruba family. He won a Rotary scholarship in 1950 and moved to the U.S. to attend Morehouse College in Atlanta, where he knew Martin Luther King Jr., who later had him perform at civil rights rallies. There he started a small drumming and dance group to challenge misconceptions about Africa. He went on to graduate studies at New York University, and by 1957 he was playing at private functions, where Columbia talent scout John Hammond noticed him.

In 1966 he and his wife, Amy, founded the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem. John Coltrane, who dedicated a composition called "Tunji" to him, gave the center money every month. Later, Olatunji worked with Grateful Dead drummer Mickey Hart on the Planet Drum ensemble, formed in 1991; its album won a Grammy that year. He died on April 6, 2003, in Salinas, California, from complications of diabetes.
keyFacts: 1927 (April 7): Born in Ajido, near Badagry, to a Yoruba family.
1950: Rotary scholarship to Morehouse College.
1959: Released Drums of Passion on Columbia Records.
1966: Co-founded the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem.
1991: Planet Drum won a Grammy.
2003 (April 6): Died in Salinas, California.
people.connectToWork: Olatunji built a group to answer the wrong ideas people held about Africa. When your materials explain a community to staff, who wrote that explanation, and how could people from that community correct it?

people.name: Tope Awotona
body: Tope Awotona was selling software when he grew frustrated with how hard it was to arrange meetings. He used his life savings and went into debt to build a scheduling tool. The tool was Calendly, which debuted in 2013 and, according to the Carnegie Corporation, has more than 20 million users in over 230 countries.

Awotona was born in 1981 in Lagos. His father, a microbiologist who had started his own company, was shot and killed in a carjacking when Awotona was 12. Three years later his mother moved the family to the Atlanta area. He studied computer science at the University of Georgia before switching to business, and earned a Bachelor of Business Administration there.

He worked at IBM and then sold software for technology companies, including EMC. His side start-ups did not succeed. He put roughly $200,000 of savings into Calendly, maxed out credit cards and drew down his 401(k), and bootstrapped the company for years; a $350 million investment in 2021 valued it at $3 billion. In 2025 he was inducted into the Technology Hall of Fame of Georgia and honored by the Carnegie Corporation of New York as a Great Immigrant. As of October 2026 Forbes lists him as Calendly's founder and CEO.
keyFacts: 1981: Born in Lagos.
Age 12: His father was killed in a carjacking; at 15 he moved with his family to the Atlanta area.
Bachelor of Business Administration, University of Georgia.
2013: Calendly debuted.
2021: A $350 million investment valued Calendly at $3 billion.
2025: Technology Hall of Fame of Georgia; Carnegie Great Immigrants honoree.
people.connectToWork: Behind this family's move was a death and a decision made years later. What do you need to know about why someone moved in order to do your job, and what is theirs to keep private?

people.name: Ijeoma Oluo
body: Ijeoma Oluo is a Seattle writer and speaker whose book So You Want to Talk About Race became a #1 New York Times bestseller.

Oluo was born in 1980 to a white mother from Wichita, Kansas, and a Black Nigerian father, a political scientist. When she was two, her father went back to his village in Nigeria; he was expected to return but stayed in touch for only a few months. Her mother raised Ijeoma and her younger brother, Ahamefule, near Seattle, working two jobs. Oluo earned a political science degree from Western Washington University and worked in tech and digital marketing before the 2012 killing of Trayvon Martin pushed her to write.

She has been editor-at-large of The Establishment, and her work has appeared in The Guardian, The New York Times and The Washington Post, among others. Her later books include Mediocre: The Dangerous Legacy of White Male America. Her honors include the American Humanist Association's 2018 Feminist Humanist Award, the 2020 Harvard Humanist of the Year Award, and a place on the 2021 TIME 100 Next list.
keyFacts: 1980: Born to a white mother from Kansas and a Nigerian father, who returned to Nigeria when she was two.
Western Washington University, political science; worked in tech and digital marketing.
Author of So You Want to Talk About Race, a #1 New York Times bestseller.

2018: Feminist Humanist Award; 2020: Harvard Humanist of the Year.
2021: TIME 100 Next.
people.connectToWork: A name or a parent's birthplace can tell you very little about how a person relates to a heritage. If your intake or outreach sorts people by name or origin, how would you let them say for themselves where they belong?

people.name: Ngozi Ezike
body: In the spring of 2020, as COVID-19 spread, Illinois residents tuned in to daily news conferences from Gov. J.B. Pritzker's administration. Standing with him was Dr. Ngozi Ezike, director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, who gave her updates in English and then in Spanish.

Ezike was born in Los Angeles, the daughter of Nigerian immigrants. Her father hoped his firstborn would become a physician. She speaks Igbo and is fluent in Spanish and French, and also speaks Swahili. She graduated with honors from Harvard, earned her medical degree at the University of California, San Diego, and completed a residency at Rush Medical Center in Chicago. She is board-certified in internal medicine and pediatrics.

For more than 15 years she worked in Cook County's public health system, including inpatient care at Stroger Hospital, medical director of the Austin Health Center on Chicago's West Side, and medical director of the Cook County Juvenile Temporary Detention Center, where she helped write its health policies. In 2019 she became the first Black woman to lead the 143-year-old state health department, serving until March 2022.

On June 13, 2022, she became president and CEO of Sinai Chicago, which CBS Chicago calls the city's largest private safety-net hospital system. Austin Weekly News described her in that role in May 2024.
keyFacts: Born in Los Angeles to Nigerian immigrant parents; speaks Igbo.
Harvard (chemistry, honors); M.D., UC San Diego; residency at Rush Medical Center.
15+ years with Cook County public health, including the Juvenile Temporary Detention Center.
2019: Director of the Illinois Department of Public Health, the first Black woman in the role.
2020: Daily COVID-19 briefings in English and Spanish.
2022: Became president and CEO of Sinai Chicago on June 13.
people.connectToWork: Ezike gave public health updates in a second language herself. Which of your important public messages reach people only in English or only in writing, and who would you ask to find out what is missing?

people.name: Wale
body: In April 2015 the Washington, D.C., rapper Wale's The Album About Nothing reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200, his second consecutive No. 1 album after The Gifted. Wale, born Olubowale Victor Akintimehin, is a D.C. native. In a 2018 interview with OkayAfrica he said, "I look at myself as a black man in America, but as a Nigerian first."

Both of his parents are Nigerian and Yoruba, from southwestern Nigeria; they arrived in the U.S. five years before he was born in 1984. The family moved to Maryland when he was ten. At Quince Orchard High School in Montgomery County he played running back as Victor Akintimehin and ran track. He took "Wale" as his stage name because many Americans found his given name hard to pronounce. He attended Robert Morris College and Virginia State University on football scholarships, transferred to Bowie State, and then left college for music. Alongside go-go, he names Michael Jackson, Jay-Z, and Nigerian stars Fela Kuti, Sunny Ade and Shina Peters among his influences.

Interscope signed him in early 2008. His debut album, Attention Deficit, came out in November 2009. Ambition (2011) reached No. 2 and The Gifted (2013) reached No. 1. "Lotus Flower Bomb," featuring Miguel, won Best Collaboration at the 2012 BET Awards and was nominated for a Grammy. In 2018 he signed with Warner Bros. Records, and in 2023 with Def Jam.
keyFacts: 1984: Born in Washington, D.C., to Yoruba Nigerian parents.
2008: Signed with Interscope; 2009: debut album Attention Deficit.
2012: "Lotus Flower Bomb" won Best Collaboration at the BET Awards.
2015 (April): The Album About Nothing reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200.
2023: Signed with Def Jam.
people.connectToWork: Wale says who he is in his own words, and he changed his name because others could not say it. What categories does your record make people choose from, and where can they describe themselves in their own words?

people.name: Ego Mang Nwokeka Ndukwe
body: A 2025 Georgia House resolution honors Ego Mang Nwokeka Ndukwe as a leader in the Nigerian and Igbo-American communities. She and her late husband, Dr. Mang Ndukwe, founded Another Chance, a Decatur, Georgia, provider of home care and day programs for people with disabilities. The company says it has served families since 2000, starting in a small office in Tucker; the resolution says she is its Chief Operating Officer.

A 2014 company release tells how it began: she gave a ride home to a disabled client walking in the rain, her employer reprimanded her, and she left that job. Her husband then proposed starting a company.

The resolution says she founded the American Coalition of Africans with disABILITIES in 2001 and served on the Governor's Council on Developmental Disabilities. In 2007 she began donating medical equipment to a hospital in her hometown of Abiriba, Nigeria, and she founded Another Chance Nigeria to provide mobility equipment and job skills training. The resolution does not say whether she is disabled herself.
keyFacts: Igbo-American leader, from Abiriba, Nigeria, by the resolution's account.
2001: Founded the American Coalition of Africans with disABILITIES.
2007: Began donating medical equipment in Abiriba.
2025: Honored in Georgia House Resolution 710.
Based in Georgia, not Minnesota.
people.connectToWork: Ndukwe was reprimanded for helping a client home in the rain. Which of your rules would stop a staff member from meeting a plain human need, and what would you do about it?

people.name: Elijah Akinyemi
body: Elijah Akinyemi was born in a small farming village in Nigeria, where his father was the village chief, and lost his sight to measles at age two. He attended the Pacelli School for the Blind and Partially Sighted Children and Igbobi College in Lagos, then came to the U.S. at 23 on a scholarship to Eastern Washington University and transferred to Portland State University. He earned a bachelor's degree in 1983 and a master's in special education in 1984.

He went home. In 1988 he became the first blind person employed in Ogun State's civil service, and over more than three decades in its education ministry he rose from Senior Education Officer to Permanent Secretary, launching programs such as a computerized Braille-book press. Beginning in 2017, working with Nigeria's National Association for the Blind and other groups, he pressed for a Nigerian law like the Americans with Disabilities Act, which Portland State's account says was signed after three attempts.
When Portland State profiled him in 2021 he had retired and was board chair of New Dawn For Disabilities Rights. He wrote an autobiography, Vision Beyond Sight.
keyFacts: Blind since age two, after measles.
Portland State University, B.A. 1983 and M.S. 1984.
1988: First blind person employed in Ogun State's civil service.
Rose to Permanent Secretary in the state education ministry.
Board chair, New Dawn For Disabilities Rights, as of 2021.
people.connectToWork: Akinyemi became the first blind person in his state's civil service. In the jobs and services you touch, who has never yet held the role, and what stands in the way?

sources.label: Portland State University, Alumni Spotlight: Elijah Akinyemi (July 20, 2021)

institutions.name: Umunne Cultural Association of Minnesota and IgboFest
institutions.type: Cultural and mutual-aid association, annual festival
institutions.location: Brooklyn Park; festival at North Hennepin Community College
body: Every August, the grounds of North Hennepin Community College in Brooklyn Park fill with music, processions and food. This is IgboFest, a free celebration of the culture of the Igbo people of southeastern Nigeria. On August 8, 2026, the festival held its 31st annual edition under the theme "preserving our cultural heritage," after a gala the evening before.

The festival is presented by the Umunne Cultural Association of Minnesota, formed by Igbo Minnesotans in 1985, according to a 2016 proclamation by Gov. Mark Dayton, which also dates the first IgboFest to 1994. It is a 501(c)(3) nonprofit whose members are Igbo-speaking Nigerians living in Minnesota. Its stated goal is to "promote and preserve our rich Igbo culture," pass that heritage to younger generations, and share it with the wider Minnesota community. It also runs educational programs and member volunteer activities, partners with other Minnesota organizations and helps Igbo students pursue careers.

Minneapolis Northwest Tourism reports attendance of more than 5,000. The 2026 festival was co-sponsored by the City of Brooklyn Park, Minneapolis Northwest Tourism and the Minnesota Humanities Center.
keyFacts: 1985: Association formed; 1994: first IgboFest.
Registered 501(c)(3); members are Igbo-speaking Nigerians in Minnesota.
Held in August at North Hennepin Community College; admission is free.
August 8, 2026: 31st annual IgboFest.
Reported attendance: more than 5,000 (Minneapolis Northwest Tourism).
institutions.connectToWork: "Nigerian" is a national identity, and this association is built around a language and a people within it. Does your data or outreach stop at the country name? How would you learn which groups a person actually belongs to, if they want you to know?

institutions.name: Olatunji Center of African Culture
institutions.type: Cultural center and school of African music and dance
body: In April 1967 the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem hosted a concert by John Coltrane, about three months before his death. Its surviving first set was later released as The Olatunji Concert: The Last Live Recording.

The center was founded in 1966 by Nigerian drummer Babatunde Olatunji and his wife, Amy. It offered low-cost classes in African music, dance and culture, part of his lifelong effort to challenge misconceptions about Africa in the United States. The Percussive Arts Society says Coltrane gave the center money every month. We did not find when it closed.
keyFacts: 1966: Founded in Harlem by Babatunde and Amy Olatunji.
Offered low-cost education in African music, dance and culture.
1967 (April): Hosted a John Coltrane concert later released as an album.
institutions.connectToWork: This center kept its lessons low in cost and had a famous backer. When you ask a cultural group to teach your staff, who pays for that work, and does the group get what it needs?

institutions.name: Redeemed Christian Church of God
institutions.location: Founded in Lagos, Nigeria; North American operations based in Texas
body: The Redeemed Christian Church of God was founded in 1952 in Lagos by Rev. Josiah Olufemi Akindayomi, beginning as a house fellowship on Willoughby Street in Ebute-Metta. Its present leader, Enoch Adeboye, was a mathematics lecturer at the University of Lagos who joined in 1973 and began by interpreting Akindayomi's sermons from Yoruba into English. He was consecrated General Overseer in January 1981.

A 2014 NPR report by John Burnett counted 758 congregations in North America, run from headquarters on farmland northeast of Dallas. James Fadele, then chairman of the North American operations, said about 100 new churches were being added each year, with a stated goal of a church in every city within a 15-minute drive of the next. According to RCCG North America, its first parish on the continent was Winners' Chapel in Detroit, started by Pastor Fadel on April 5, 1991, and by December 2015 it reported more than 800 parishes. As of October 2026 its website names Pastor James Fadel as Continental Overseer. NPR and the church spell the name differently.

RCCG North America's 2020 list of parishes no longer in RCCG (USA) includes Strong Tower Parish, Minneapolis (ZIP 55413), so it should not be presented as an RCCG parish. An older church directory listed it at 697 Northeast 13th Avenue.
keyFacts: 1952: Founded in Lagos by Rev. Josiah Olufemi Akindayomi.
1981: Enoch Adeboye became General Overseer.
1991 (April 5): First North American parish, in Detroit, by the church's account.
2014: 758 congregations in North America (NPR).
2015: More than 800 parishes (RCCG North America).
institutions.connectToWork: A person's nearest support may be a congregation your agency has never heard of. How would you ask whether faith or a congregation matters to someone, without assuming that it does, and without contacting it unless they ask?

institutions.name: Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities
aliases: MN Community of African People with Disabilities
body: The Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities is a Minneapolis nonprofit founded in 2014. Its own site says it was founded by disabled East African American adults; a 2023 profile in a Minnesota House committee document says it was founded by an East African immigrant.

That profile says its mission is to break down generational trauma and language and cultural barriers that affect immigrants, especially those with disabilities, to help families feel confident asking for help, and to support caregivers. Its site lists basic and intensive support services, quality of life skills, employment help and day support. It serves African people broadly and is not specific to Nigerians. The most recent news post on its site is from November 2023, so call before you refer someone.
keyFacts: 2014: Founded in Minnesota.
Serves African people with disabilities and their caregivers.
2023: Profiled in a Minnesota House committee document supporting bill H.F. 2583.
Pan-African, not Nigerian-specific.
institutions.connectToWork: A provider can be close to a community and still not be the right fit for a person. When you offer a culturally specific service, how do you make sure it is a choice alongside the others, and not the only option you mention?

sources.label: Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities
Minnesota House committee document with organization profiles, including MNCAPD (2023)

disability.intro: This is background for preparing questions. It does not describe any person or family. Nigerian here means people who identify with Nigeria or its diaspora, from many ethnic groups, including Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa, and from Christian, Muslim and other faiths. We did not find a study of disability among Nigerian Minnesotans or Nigerian Americans. Most of the research below comes from parents in Nigeria, one study comes from African immigrant parents in Ireland, and nearly all of it is about autism in children.
questions: How do you and your family understand what is going on? What words do you use for it, in English and in any other language?
Has anyone given you a diagnosis or a label? Who gave it, and has it helped or got in the way?
What would you want a label or assessment to open up for you? Is there anything you want it to avoid?
What have you been told about the condition, and what do you think might help?
Who do you want involved in decisions and meetings, including relatives in Nigeria who might join by phone? Is there anyone you do not want involved?
Which language do you prefer for medical and legal topics? Would you like an interpreter, even if you speak English well?
Which words do you find hurtful, and which do you prefer?
Who helps with care day to day, and do they have the support they need?
Is a congregation, mosque or hometown association part of your support? Would you like it connected to your services, or kept separate?
What do you want others in your community to know, and what do you want kept private?
What would you like explained about how Minnesota services work, such as who sees the records and what things cost?

context.heading: What a Lagos study asked parents
body: Oduyemi and colleagues surveyed 230 parents of autistic children at a clinic in Lagos, Nigeria, and interviewed six mothers, in a study published in 2021. Parents most often named birth complications (31.7 percent), family history (16.9 percent) and head injury (16.5 percent) as the cause; 13.5 percent said they did not know. Only 1.3 percent had "good" overall knowledge of autism as the authors measured it. Most parents were mothers (76 percent), and 72 percent were Yoruba, so it is not a picture of all Nigerians.

In that sample, 53 percent reported negative experiences with others and 83.5 percent reported self-stigma. Health workers were the most common source of information (48.3 percent), then media (31.7 percent), with family at 9.6 percent and friends at 6.1 percent. Some parents said they had accepted their fate or left things to God, which the authors present as a way of coping. All the interviews were with mothers, because the fathers declined. The study shows who took part, and it does not show who makes decisions. None of this describes a family you meet in Minnesota.

sources.label: Oduyemi and colleagues, BMC Psychology (2021)

context.heading: A survey of parents across Nigeria
body: A Texas Tech poster reports a survey of 247 parents in Nigeria: 74.5 percent were women, 88.7 percent lived in cities, 57.1 percent were Christian, 39.3 percent Muslim and 2.8 percent followed traditional religion. Stigma was significantly associated with whether parents believed autism could be cured and whether they felt others believed it could be passed on; the poster does not say in which direction. The authors report higher stigma among parents who first sought help from traditional institutions or had less education. Religion was not significantly associated with stigma. A survey like this cannot say that one thing led to another.

For your own preparation: if a person or family raises a worry that a condition can spread, or that a parent caused it, be ready with clear information, and ask whether a mother or other main caregiver has support.

sources.label: Ihenagwam, Hamrick, Wheeler and Iwuji, Texas Tech Burkhart Center poster
Oduyemi and colleagues, BMC Psychology (2021)

context.heading: African immigrant parents in Ireland
body: A 2023 University College Cork thesis by Jingwa interviewed 10 parents of disabled children from Nigeria, Cameroon and South Africa living in Ireland, and 10 health and social care professionals. Parents valued the services they received, but relationships with professionals carried tension and ambivalence. Unfamiliarity with the health system and structural barriers made services harder to use, and professionals said they did not feel equipped. Ireland is not Minnesota. Use it as a prompt to look at your own system.

sources.label: Jingwa, PhD thesis, University College Cork (2023)

context.heading: Words and language
body: An essay in the Nigerian newspaper Leadership discusses Hausa terms: nakasa for disability, with makaho (blind) and kurma (deaf) as examples, and bukata ta musamman for "special needs." It quotes a saying, nakasa ba kasawa ba ce, "disability is not inability." These come from Nigeria, not from Minnesota families. We did not find reliable sources for Yoruba, Igbo or Nigerian Pidgin terms, so ask the person and the interpreter.
English is an official language of Nigeria, and fluency varies. Do not assume a person needs an interpreter, and do not assume they do not.

sources.label: Leadership (Nigeria), Misconception of the concept of disability and special needs in Hausa thought

context.heading: What we could not find
body: We found no research on the roles of extended family or elders among Nigerian Americans, and no Nigerian-specific disability organization in Minnesota. The closest we found is the Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities, which is pan-African.

sources.label: Minnesota House committee document with organization profiles, including MNCAPD (2023)

communityRoutes.name: Minnesota Community of African People with Disabilities
communityRoutes.purpose: A Minneapolis provider for African people with disabilities and their caregivers, listing support services, employment help and day support. Not specific to Nigerians. Call first, 612-345-4786, to ask whether it serves the person and is taking referrals. A family's own choice, never a replacement for your agency's duties.

organizations.intro: These are starting points for learning, and the list is not complete. Listing here says nothing about who a person trusts, and no group speaks for everyone. Minnesota Compass (ACS 2020 to 2024) counts 21,206 Nigerian Minnesotans (plus or minus 3,847) and gives a 2024 best estimate of 25,310 (plus or minus 9,024), with wide margins. Compass also reports that 32 percent of Nigerian-born Minnesotans have been in the U.S. five years or fewer, the highest share among the immigrant groups it lists. A 2016 governor's proclamation speaks of "thousands of Igbo residents," with no stated method. CCX Media reported in 2019 that Brooklyn Park and Brooklyn Center are home to one of the largest African populations in Minnesota. MIND lists the Igbo Women League of Minnesota (about 30 years old), the Egba Descendants Association of Minnesota (founded 2002), Egbe Omo Oduduwa Minnesota (a Yoruba association founded 1995), the Edo Association of Minnesota, the Anioma Cultural Association, the Ibadan Descendants' Union, the Ijebu Descendants Association and Ekitileto. Eko Club Minnesota, an association of Lagosians, was founded in 2004. We did not find a Nigerian Muslim association. That does not mean none exists, and groups may organize in ways that do not show up online.

entries.name: Association of Nigerian Nurses in Minnesota
entries.purpose: Describes itself as an umbrella for Nigerian nurses associations in Minnesota, working to advance nursing and reduce health disparities. Its site shows a 20th anniversary gala, a newsletter begun in March 2024, and continuing education courses available through December 2026.

entries.name: Minnesota Institute for Nigeria's Development
entries.purpose: The Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development calls itself the umbrella for the Nigerian community in Minnesota since 1994. It holds an open general meeting the first Sunday of each month at Camphor Memorial Methodist Church in St. Paul, lists an October Independence celebration and a summer picnic, and is raising money for a community center. A 2023 profile named Dr. Fatima Lawson as vice president.
entries.linkLabel: Minnesota Institute for Nigerian Development, official site

entries.name: Nigerian Student Association, University of Minnesota
entries.purpose: A registered student group that aims to foster a community of Nigerian students in the diaspora and to preserve and promote Nigerian culture. Its page shows 6 officers and 21 members, and no upcoming events.

entries.name: Brooklyn Park sister city relationship with Nigeria
entries.purpose: The city says it has built sister city relationships since 2012 with cities in Liberia, The Gambia and Nigeria. Mshale reported in October 2024 that the city celebrated its Nigerian sister city, Udu, and honored actor Richard Mofe-Damijo.

entries.name: Mshale
entries.purpose: Described by MPR News as Minnesota's longest running newspaper serving African immigrants, founded in the mid-1990s by Tom Gitaa, who came from Kenya. It reports on Nigerian Minnesotans, including IgboFest.

entries.name: Sahan Journal
entries.purpose: Founded in 2019 by Mukhtar Ibrahim. Reports for and about Minnesota's immigrants and communities of color. Not specific to Nigerians.

entries.name: Nigerians in Diaspora Organisation Americas
entries.purpose: Its rival groups agreed to unite at an extraordinary meeting on November 16, 2024, in Bloomington, Minnesota, with more than 20 U.S. chapter presidents taking part, ThisDay reported. We did not find an official website.

entries.name: Association of Nigerian Physicians in the Americas
entries.location: United States, Canada and the Caribbean
entries.purpose: Incorporated in 1995. Says it represents more than 8,000 physicians, dentists and allied health professionals, and lists more than 900 active members and 25 local chapters. It held its 32nd annual convention in Chicago in 2026.

entries.name: World Igbo Congress
entries.purpose: Founded in 1994 in Houston, says its site, to unify Igbo people, especially in the diaspora, and to promote Igbo culture and development. It posted a statement in June 2026.

entries.name: Nigerian-American Multicultural Council
entries.purpose: Founded in 2011. Works to keep Nigerian heritage alive for Nigerian Americans born or raised in the U.S., with civic, professional, mentoring and cultural programs. It is regional, listed here as one example from outside Minnesota.

entries.name: Channels Television
entries.purpose: A Nigerian news broadcaster that publishes in English online.

entries.name: Arise News
entries.location: Studios in London and New York
entries.purpose: A 24-hour news channel run by Arise Global Media, with a strong focus on Africa.

entries.name: Punch
entries.purpose: A Nigerian daily newspaper with news online, in English.

entries.name: Premium Times
entries.purpose: A Nigerian news outlet covering news, investigations, business, health and opinion, in English.

entries.name: ThisDay
entries.purpose: A Nigerian daily that has covered diaspora groups, including the 2024 meeting in Bloomington, Minnesota.

entries.name: BBC News Pidgin, Yoruba, Igbo and Hausa
entries.purpose: News in Nigerian languages. The link goes to Pidgin, launched in August 2017, with Yoruba and Igbo then planned for the next year. The others are at bbc.com/yoruba, bbc.com/igbo and bbc.com/hausa.

entries.name: Sahara Reporters
entries.purpose: A news site from Sahara Reporters, Inc., that centers on Nigeria and encourages citizen reporting on corruption and government misconduct. It has covered diaspora groups.

entries.name: Voice of Nigeria
entries.purpose: A state-owned international broadcaster, established in 1961, broadcasting in 8 languages. It is the Nigerian government's outlet, so read it as such.

entries.name: Peoples Gazette
entries.purpose: A Nigerian news site. In March 2022 it carried a News Agency of Nigeria report that the consulate in New York planned a passport outreach in Minnesota, expecting about 400 Nigerians, after requests had gone unanswered since 2018 and 2019.
